We're working on both the spec and the code, as a chain. This first step changes the spec only, located in ./spec; the code is changed in the next step.

Write the spec so it describes the application as it should be once the prompt is met, and constrains the code. Once you finish, the spec will be built and the same prompt sent to a coding agent, with your reply, to change the code to match it; so end your reply by saying what you changed in the spec and which anchors the code should follow.

When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read .suspense/suspense-fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.

Before creating or editing any .pi file, read .suspense/fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.

Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton check` and fix every error it reports, then run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under .claude/reference, not by reading the source again. Never finish with a spec that `piton check` or `piton build` reports errors in.

Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to .suspense/history/1791132843-ProjectsCreatedWithWindowsAdmin.understanding.md, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.

### Shape

#### Description

A form titled "New Project", with a close button, holding the project's name, where it goes, the template it starts from, and its Belay options, and along the bottom a "Cancel" button and a primary "New" button that creates it. The name field has focus when the form opens.

#### Layout

The form's body is two columns of equal width side by side, top aligned, scrolling together when the panel is too short for them. The first holds the project itself: its name, its location, the Git checkbox, and the spec, code, and shape roots. The second holds what it starts from and what it's written for: the template, then the agents.

#### Name

A "Name" field for the project's name, which is also the name of its folder. It can't be empty, contain a slash or backslash, or be "." or "..".

#### Location

A "Location" row showing the folder the project's folder goes in, with a "Browse…" button beside it. It starts in the folder holding the open project, or the user's home folder when no project is open. Beneath it, muted, the full path of the folder that will be created.
Browse opens a [FolderBrowserScope](../../ui/components/folder-browser/index.md#folder-browser-scope) in place of the form, titled "Choose where the project goes" and starting in the current location. A new folder for the project to go in can be created from there. Choosing a folder makes it the location, and choosing or cancelling goes back to the form, just as it was left.

#### Git

Beneath the location, an "Initialize a Git repository" checkbox, checked to start with. Its label is shown in full, like the agents' labels.

#### Templates

At the top of the second column, a "Template" group lists the templates a project can start from, one row each, in order, as radio buttons, only one chosen at a time: each shows the template's name, and beneath it, muted, what it holds. The first is chosen to start with. There are two:

- "Base", with nothing more than the project needs: an empty index.pi in the spec root
- "Scope, concept, and shape", which seeds the spec root with a lib of the abstract scope, concept, and shape anchors a spec is written with, each in a file of its own, an index.pi in the lib exporting them all, an index.pi in the spec root using the lib, and an example scope, with its concept and shape, to start from

The templates are folders in the project-templates folder at the root of the Suspense repository, one per template, and are built into the application when it is built, so changing or adding one changes what the next build offers. Each holds a template.json giving its name, its description, and its place in the order, and, in a spec folder, the files it seeds the spec root with, laid out as they are to be written there. A template with no spec folder seeds nothing more than the base does.

#### Agents

Beneath the template, in the second column, an "Agents" group of checkboxes, one per agent Belay has an adapter for, each with the directory it writes into: "Claude Code" (.claude), "OpenCode" (.opencode), and "Codex" (.codex). Only Claude Code starts checked. At least one must be checked.
Each checkbox's label is shown in full beside it, vertically centred on it, with room below its baseline so the bottoms of letters like p and y, and of the brackets, are never cut off.

#### Folders

Three fields, each a path relative to the project folder: "Spec root", starting as ./spec; "Code root", starting as ./src; and "Shape root", starting as ./spec/shape, which can be left empty to go without one. Spec root and code root can't be empty. A path is written with a leading ./ whether or not it was typed with one, and none can be absolute or climb out of the project with "..".

#### Config

The piton.config.pi written for the project uses @piton/config and @piton/belay. It exports a piton-config anchor named after the project, its name in PascalCase from its letters and digits, or "Project" when that leaves nothing or starts with a digit, whose root is the spec root, whose entry is index.pi in the spec root, and whose only framework is a belay-config anchor named BelayConfiguration. That anchor has the code root as its codeRoot, the shape root as its shapeRoot unless there is none, and an adapter for each checked agent, in the order they are

##### Listed

ClaudeCodeAdapter, OpenCodeAdapter, and CodexAdapter, each

imported from @piton/belay. The file is written in Piton's canonical formatting.
With OpenCode checked, an opencode.json is also written in the project's folder, unless there is one: it lists the AGENTS.md files under the code root, as `<code root>/**/AGENTS.md`, as instructions, since OpenCode doesn't load the guidance Belay places throughout the code on its own, and denies the skills whose names start with x-, the ones Belay writes for commands, so OpenCode doesn't also offer them as ordinary skills.

#### Creating

"New" is disabled, with a tooltip saying why, until the name is valid, the paths are, and an agent is checked, and while a project is being created. A field that isn't valid says why beneath it once something has been typed in it.
Pressing it creates the project's folder, and any folders leading to it, then writes piton.config.pi there, creates the spec root, writes the chosen template's files into it, or an empty index.pi when the template gives none, and creates the code root and any shape root. It never overwrites anything: a folder that already holds a piton.config.pi is refused, a file already in the spec root is left as it is, and folders that already exist are kept. A project created from either template builds with `piton build` straight away.
With "Initialize a Git repository" checked, once the rest is created the project's folder is made a Git repository with `git init`, unless it already is the top of one, and a .gitignore is written there ignoring what Suspense keeps for this machine alone rather than for the project, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. An existing .gitignore is left as it is. Nothing is committed. If Git fails, the project still opens, and a warning notification says the repository couldn't be initialized, and why.
Once created, the project opens as if opened with the [OpenProjectScope](../project/open-project/index.md#open-project-scope), becoming the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope), and the form closes. If anything fails, the form stays open and says what went wrong above its buttons.

content.content:
The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command, and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.
On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user, with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages.

        Every file and folder the application creates belongs to the user
        running it, as one the user made in Explorer or a terminal would, on
        every platform, so the user never has to take ownership of anything,
        or change its permissions, to edit, move, or delete it, or for git,
        piton, or the harness to use it. That goes for a new project's folder
        and everything written into it, the project's data under .suspense,
        the files a task or the editor writes, and the application's own
        files, as its preferences.

        On Windows, the application never asks to run as administrator: its
        build declares that it runs with the rights of whoever starts it, as
        invoked, and never requires elevation, nor does its installer start
        it elevated once it is installed, nor its self-update when it starts
        the new version. Should it be run elevated all the same, as from an
        administrator's terminal, what it creates is still the user's: each
        file and folder is made owned by the user who is signed in, never by
        the Administrators group, and takes the permissions it inherits from
        the folder it is in, never permissions of its own. The same holds for
        what the programs it starts create, git's repository included, so git
        never refuses a project for being owned by someone else.
        Nothing the application creates is ever left owned by Administrators,
        SYSTEM, or another account.

use /lib
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/project-locations import ProjectLocationsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from /scope/settings-window import SettingsWindowScope
from /scope/spec-build import SpecBuildScope

export scope ContainerEnvironmentScope:
    concept: {ContainerEnvironmentConcept}

concept ContainerEnvironmentConcept:
    pitch:
        A container the application owns, that a run of the harness works
        in, so each mode sees only what it may use. What a run can read or
        change comes from what is mounted into its container, never from its
        prompt, a deny rule, or a guard: a container with no code in it can't
        read the code or change it, whatever the harness is and whatever it
        tries.

    shape: {ContainerEnvironmentShape}

shape ContainerEnvironmentShape:
    description:
        Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps and spec follow-up, and
        questions from the Ask tab always run in a container, and are the
        only runs that do. Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code step always
        run on the host, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, with their
        protected locations, and never need Podman. Freeform tasks always
        run on the host, and so do the application's own runs, the one-off runs, the
        palette's file search, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt
        titles, which change nothing.

        Whatever runs in a container, the application itself still works on
        the host: it builds the spec before a task, takes the task's
        snapshots and lists the files it changed, shows diffs, and makes
        commits there, as ever.

    runtime:
        The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command,
        and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's
        command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its
        standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as
        a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its
        container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.

        On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user,
        with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the
        user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its
        containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages.

    missingPodman:
        Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a
        container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task,
        a Chain prompt's spec steps, or a question. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed
        does, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, or as one whose spec
        build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to
        run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's
        installation instructions for the platform it is running on:

        - on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
        - on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
        - on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux

        A Code task, and a Chain prompt's code step, never needs Podman, and
        runs whether it is installed or not.

    podmanMachine:
        On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is
        running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and
        offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs
        `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is
        one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a
        button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`.
        Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it
        runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending
        it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux
        there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.

    podmanAccess:
        Where `podman` is installed, and on macOS and Windows its machine is
        running, but the application can't get Podman to run a container
        for it, as where the user may not use it, its rootless setup is
        missing, as the user's subordinate IDs, or it can't reach its
        service or machine, the run fails because of Podman, never because
        of the harness: it never reads "the harness reported an error", or
        any message that blames the harness or leaves the cause unnamed.
        The application tells this apart from a harness that ran and
        failed by what Podman itself reports, its exit status and what it
        prints before the harness starts in the container. The task's or
        question's output says plainly that the harness couldn't be run
        because Podman couldn't be accessed, and then gives, as written,
        what Podman printed about why. It is never run on the host instead.
        The same holds for a `podman build` of its image that fails for
        that reason: it says Podman couldn't be accessed, not only that
        the build failed.

    image:
        Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`,
        and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness
        commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the
        version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its
        latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions
        changes.

        Each command the image holds has to run in it, not only be there. The
        build ends by running each one's version command in the image, as
        `piton --version`, and a build where one fails, as a piton built
        against a newer C library than the image has, fails, saying which
        command couldn't run and what it printed. An image whose piton can't
        run is never used, so a Spec run is never sent where it can't run
        `piton build` to check its work.

        A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own,
        `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add what
        its runs in a container need, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says. The
        project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when
        the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the
        project's runs use the default image.

        While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows
        "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes
        to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.

    mounts:
        What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing
        else from the host. The project is mounted at the same fixed path in
        the container, `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, on every platform, each location given
        at its place relative to the project directory under `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`,
        and the run works in `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`. So a harness that keys its
        sessions on its working directory, as Claude Code does, finds them
        again after the project moves, whatever its path on the host. What
        each kind of run is given, as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} names
        the locations, follows.

        spec:
            A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the
            spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the
            harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can
            run `piton build` itself; the project's `.piton` directory, which
            holds the build's manifest of the files it owns, read and write,
            for the same reason, bound in from the project itself, never an
            empty, temporary, or copied one, so the manifest a build in the
            container starts from is the host's, and what it writes there is
            the host's next build's, the application creating the directory
            in the project first where it isn't there; the Suspense fluency file, read
            only; the fluency file, read
            only;
            piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file,
            read and write. Never the code location: in its place, an empty
            scratch directory, writable, that nothing else sees and that goes
            with the container, so `piton build` finds the code location it
            places the shape's guidance in.

        question:
            A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the spec
            location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read
            only, so it can run `piton slice` in its container, and the
            Suspense fluency file, read only. Nothing is
            writable but the harness's own volume and the questions' sessions
            folder. Where one of the code location and the spec location
            holds the other, both are still mounted, read only, and neither
            is hidden from the question by the other.

        Each run is also given its own conversation's sessions folder, read
        and write, as Volumes says, and nothing of any other conversation's.

        Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the
        user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the
        project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code
        location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without
        the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it, unless
        the run is given the one held as well, as a question is given both
        the code location and the spec location.

        A task's understanding file is mounted on its own, never the history
        folder it is in, so a run sees no other task's record. Since a file
        has to be there to be mounted, the application writes it empty just
        before the run, and an empty understanding file is shown as one not
        written yet is.

    paths:
        On every platform, every path a run reports from its container is
        mapped back to its host path, `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl` standing for the project
        directory, before it is shown or opened anywhere: the referenced spec
        in the right sidebar, file links in the task's output, its
        understanding file, the files it changed, and what its tool calls
        touched. Only a path that is `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, or begins with
        `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl/`, is mapped, never text that merely holds it, as
        `/workspace-old`. A path
        that maps to nothing on the host is shown as the run gave it, and
        opens nothing.

    volumes:
        The only volumes are one per harness, for its login and settings,
        ~/.claude, ~/.codex, or OpenCode's data directory as the harness
        keeps it, owned and named by the application and shared by every
        project, so each harness is logged in once for all of them. Losing
        one costs only a login.

        The harness's sessions are never kept in a volume. They are kept in
        the project, in `.suspense/sessions/`, as the @{ProjectDataScope}
        says, one folder per conversation: `spec` for the spec lane's, and
        `questions` for the Ask tab's questions. Each run mounts only its own
        conversation's folder, read and write, where the harness keeps its
        sessions under its home, as Claude Code's ~/.claude/projects, never
        `.suspense/sessions/` as a whole, so no run sees another
        conversation's sessions. The application creates the folder before
        the run if it isn't there. So a conversation carries on across runs,
        restarts of the application, and moves of the project, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says.

        Losing the project's sessions folder costs only the conversations'
        context: the next run starts a new conversation, as when a session
        can't be resumed. Sessions kept in volumes before this aren't carried
        over; each conversation starts fresh.

    loggingIn:
        When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs
        its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows
        a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the
        command prints. Any login URL the command prints opens in the host's
        browser. Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has
        a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where
        the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port
        is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a
        device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is
        sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is
        cancelled or fails.

        The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed
        there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every
        run. The @{SettingsWindowScope} shows whether each harness is logged
        in in its container, and can log it in again.

    guards:
        A run in a container has no protected locations, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} names them: it isn't guarded, and its
        harness is given no rule against reading or editing any location,
        since nothing it mustn't touch is there. Its prompts, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, name only what it can see. Runs on
        the host keep their protected locations as ever.

    specBuild:
        A Spec run can run `piton build` in its container, to check its work
        in the refreshed reference, and that build succeeds whenever the spec
        is sound: it owns the reference files it finds, through the
        manifest in the mounted `.piton` directory, and places the shape's
        guidance in the scratch directory standing in for the code location,
        where it goes nowhere. A build there that fails fails only because of
        the spec, never because of what the container leaves out, so its
        errors are the run's own to fix. Once a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step is over,
        however it ended, the application runs `piton build` on the host, as
        the @{SpecBuildScope} says, so the host's reference and shape guidance
        are those of the spec as the run left it.

with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the
user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its
-        containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages.

content.text:
I couldn't find the cause in the spec. It said nothing about who owns the files Suspense creates, so I added a rule that everything it creates belongs to the signed-in user. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 79 files, and the new text is in the refreshed reference.

**The two likely causes:**
- **Suspense running as administrator.** Files an elevated process creates on Windows end up owned by the Administrators group.
- **Files written from the Podman machine.** A container run writes into the Windows project folder from inside a virtual machine, which can leave odd ownership.

The spec now rules out both, but the code step should confirm which one actually happened to you.

## What changed in the spec

**1. New "File Ownership" section** (`.claude/reference/scope/application/index.md#file-ownership`)
- **Who owns what:** every file and folder Suspense creates belongs to the user, as if you'd made it yourself, on every platform. That covers new project folders and their contents, `.suspense` data, files written by tasks or the editor, and Suspense's own files such as preferences.
- **No elevation on Windows:** Suspense declares that it runs with the rights of whoever starts it and never requires elevation. Its installer and self-update must not start it elevated either.
- **If it runs elevated anyway:** each file and folder it creates is still owned by the signed-in user, not Administrators, and takes its permissions from the folder it's in. The same applies to the programs it starts, including git's repository, so git never refuses a project as owned by someone else.
- **Never left behind:** nothing is ever left owned by Administrators, SYSTEM or another account.

**2. New Project** (`.claude/reference/scope/new-project/index.md#creating`): everything the form creates, Git repository included, belongs to you, so the project can be edited, built and committed right away with no ownership to take.

**3. Containers** (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md#description`): on macOS and Windows, container runs act as you rather than root inside the Podman machine. Files they write into a folder mounted from Windows are yours and inherit that folder's permissions.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791132843-ProjectsCreatedWithWindowsAdmin.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `ApplicationScope`: `#file-ownership`. This covers the Windows build's setting that it runs without elevation, the installer, self-update, and setting ownership when Suspense finds itself elevated.
- `NewProjectScope`: `#creating`.
- `ContainerEnvironmentScope`: `#description`, for the user Podman runs containers as on Windows and macOS.
